speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SPEAKERS OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
By leave of the house may I make reference to an unusual circumstance. We frequently have distinguished members of other legislatures with us in the House of Commons but I think this is the first occasion on which we have had no less than six presiding officers of Canadian legislatures with us in the gallery. I do not know whether hon. members will regard this as a good thing; it depends upon the view they take of speakers.
I once heard Lord Attlee at a dinner at which there were a great many Speakers of the commonwealth present trying to find a collective term to describe them. He chose "a spout of Speakers".
I assure hon. members that our distinguished guests are here this morning to observe and not to admonish. On your behalf I take the opportunity of welcoming to the House of Commons Hon. William Murdoch, Speaker of the Ontario legislature; Hon. H. A. Veniot, Speaker of the Nova Scotia legislature; Hon. Mr. Richard, Speaker of the New Brunswick legislature; Hon. A. W. Harrison, Speaker of the Manitoba legislature; Hon. J. R. McLean, Speaker of the Prince Edward Island legislature and Hon. Peter Dawson, Speaker of the Alberta legislature. In addition, we have Hon. Frank Connors, member of the legislative council of Quebec representing the president of the council; Mr. Oswald Parent representing the speaker of the legislative assembly of Quebec; Mr. F. A. Dewhurst from Saskatchewan who, if reports can be believed, may soon become the Speaker of the Saskatchewan legislature; Mr. W. McKay, clerk of the Prince Edward Island legislature is here. British Columbia and Newfoundland are not represented because their legislatures are in session.
These gentlemen are here to attend the meeting of the Canadian area council of the commonwealth parliamentary association which comprises all of the Canadian branches.
May I also extend our welcome to the wives who are accompanying the members of the council.

The point is made that this is a matter of personal explanation which is permissible, of course, where a member has been misquoted or his remarks have been misinterpreted and this arises in the course of debate. There is a reference in Beauchesne, citation 113, in these words:
Members often raise so-called "questions of privilege" on matters which should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in the debates or the proceedings of the house. A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament. It should be dealt with by a motion giving the house power to impose a reparation or apply a remedy.
And further down the page:
But a dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
That is the normal practice and unless the Minister of Justice considers that the breach of privilege which he asserts goes beyond a matter of difference as to facts and involves misconduct on the part of the Leader of the Opposition, which would arise if there were a deliberate misleading of the house, then he seems to come within the citation. But it is possible for privilege to arise where a member has given wrong information to the house. If he has misled the house knowingly, then of course that would probably be the subject of a motion, referred to a committee and dealt with as a matter affecting the privileges of the house. Having said that, I will hear the minister further.

I have a brief statement to make concerning the second commonwealth educational conference which was convened in New Delhi on January 11 and is ending today.
It will be recalled that the idea of a formal scheme for commonwealth educational co-operation was first put forward by Canada at the 1958 Montreal conference of Commonwealth trade and economic ministers. Following that initiative by Canada a commonwealth educational conference was held at Oxford, England, in July 1959 where the commonwealth education program was launched. Since that time it has developed most successfully and has met to a most rewarding degree the lofty expectations of its founders. Canada has played an important part in the implementation of the program which the government regards as a strong force for better understanding and for continued close relations among members of the commonwealth.
I have here a list of the students attending universities in Canada under this scheme and of those from Canada attending commonwealth universities abroad. Perhaps that list could be printed at the end of my statement. I would point out that there are now 184 scholars from other parts of the commonwealth in Canada and 61 Canadians studying abroad. The reason for the difference in numbers is, of course, that there are not the university facilities in many of these commonwealth countries which we are fortunate enough to have in Canada.
At this recent meeting in New Delhi, Canada was represented by a full delegation

Commonwealth Educational Conference headed by our High Commissioner in London, Hon. George A. Drew, who also led the Canadian delegation to the first conference at Oxford and has followed the development of the commonwealth education program with a close and expert interest. The delegation also consisted of representatives of Canadian educational institutions and of national educational organizations which included provincial representation.
I have here a list of delegates which, perhaps, could also be printed at the end of my statement. Hon. members will realize that it comprises a very distinguished group.
The delegation participated effectively in all matters of common interest which came under discussion. Many recommendations were put forward for the continued development of the commonwealth education program and for improvements in its operation. These recommendations will now be submitted to member governments for consideration with a view to implementation.
I am sure hon. members will be glad to learn that the Canadian government has extended an invitation to hold the third commonwealth educational conference in Canada. This will probably be held in the year 1964. The offer is being recommended for acceptance by the delegates meeting in New Delhi.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW NAME FOR TRANSPORT FLEET
speechtext:
The government has decided that the main Department of Transport fleet of ships will in future be known as the Canadian coastguard. The decision to adopt the new name for the fleet was taken in recognition of the tremendous expansion it has undergone in the past several years in the scope of its operations, in the number of vessels and in the standards of operation that have been achieved. This fleet has been known as the Canadian marine service.
At the same time it has been decided to adopt a new colour scheme for its vessels and a distinctive insignia for their funnels. The ships will have red hulls with white superstructure and funnels instead of the former black, white and yellow combination. A moderately stylized red maple leaf and band on the white funnels will make them easily recognizable at a distance as Canadian coastguard vessels.
The use of red for the hulls is of significant practical utility, particularly for icebreakers, as they will be more easily seen from vessels they may be escorting and by pilots of our own helicopters under conditions of poor visibility. The same need for visibility and ready identification applies to the Canadian coastguard vessels which are on search and rescue duties.
New types of uniforms will be issued which will provide comfortable and smart clothing appropriate to the conditions of the service. These uniforms are modelled on the wartime battle dress and berets are to be provided.
The essentially civilian character of the fleet will remain unchanged. Pilot vessels and canal craft will continue to be operated as separate units by the appropriate divisions of the department.

611. Payments to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely, $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $42,000,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this vote carry?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Acting Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I regret that illness prevents the Minister of Agriculture from presenting this estimate to provide for an acreage payment to western grain producers. Thus it falls upon me to do so and I take advantage of the opportunity to compliment you, Mr. Chairman, on your appointment to the important post you hold. I know of no one who could fill the position in a more distinguished manner.
It will be recalled that because of the serious financial position, particularly of the smaller western grain producers, and also due to the absence of a two-price system for wheat, previous acreage payments were made in 1958 and 1960. The reasons why this form of assistance was decided upon in those years were given at length by the Prime Minister and myself when it was originally proposed and debated in this committee. Perhaps I should refer to the Hansard reports in which those debates are recorded so that any members of the committee who would like to refresh their memories in regard to these matters will know where to find them readily.
Supply-Agriculture
They are in Hansard of August 30 and September 6, 1958, and of August 8 and 9, 1960.
I shall not repeat the comprehensive statements made on those occasions but will very briefly sum up the principal reasons why it was decided to provide this particular form of assistance to western farmers. After a careful examination of various programs suggested to improve the income position of these farmers it became quite apparent this was the most equitable and practical method of meeting the difficulty. Second, this method ensures that the smaller, worse-off farmers receive the greatest proportion of benefit from the money provided, and this is one of the main considerations which must be borne in mind in extending assistance of that kind.
Third, assistance by acreage does not stimulate production of particular commodities, thus creating and increasing surpluses which have been found difficult to dispose of in the past. In this connection it is encouraging to record that we have made very great progress in the last year or more in disposing of our large surplus of grain, particularly wheat. Nevertheless a system of assistance which would considerably encourage the production of certain of these grains and cause a move away from a more diversified type of agriculture in western Canada would be a step in the wrong direction.
Fourth, acreage payments are a type of payment which does not serve as an impediment to the marketing of agricultural commodities or to free trade in them, while many of the alternative schemes of assistance which have been suggested would have that undesirable feature. In view of the fact we are dependant to such a great extent on exports of our agricultural products, that is something which we must always keep in mind in any agricultural assistance we institute.
This year there is a very important additional reason why a payment of this kind should be made. It is to be found in the reduced farm income, particularly of people in certain areas of western Canada due to the drought which took place there last year. This drought in the long run did not prove as devastating and serious as at one time was believed would be the case, but nevertheless it did have very serious effects which are particularly apparent in the income position of many farmers in western Canada. How serious that is can be shown by comparing the average wheat yield this year with that of previous years. During the past crop year the average wheat yield is estimated to have been 10.4 bushels per acre, whereas for the previous five years it was 19.7 bushels per

Supply-Agriculture
acre. In other words, this year's yield was not very much more than half of what had been secured on the average in the previous five years. This gives a good indication of the situation in which many farmers will find themselves, and demonstrates the necessity of assistance in the form proposed.
The payments to be made under the authority of this vote will follow the same pattern as the two previous payments. That is, each producer holding a wheat board delivery permit will receive $1 for each cultivated acre listed in the permit, up to a maximum of $200. Payments will be made to holders of delivery permits for the current crop year, that is 1961-62, and it is estimated that approximately 235,000 payments will be made.

I do not
wish to be rude but will the minister clarify one matter? Do I understand that while payments will be made on the permits books, a person with two or three permit books will be entitled to one payment only? If so can he say how a cross check will be made as there were a number of extra payments made last time by error?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The payments will be made through the wheat board as they were on the two previous occasions and the checking will be done on the basis of their records. Every effort, of course, will be made to ensure that a man who may happen to hold two permits will not be paid on both of them. On the last occasion there were some cases where this happened and repayment was requested. In the final check of every case where an error of that sort was made, repayment was sought. It is always possible that errors can be made in cases of people with similar names, but I do not think that is a material matter so far as the scheme generally is concerned. However, there are several matters which caused questions to be raised at the time payments were made previously. I might mention a few of them so that there may be no doubt in anyone's mind as to the situation at the present time. The first of these matters is in connection with joint permits, that is, a permit in which more than one person is shown as the actual producer. This covers partnerships and things of that sort. Where payments are made to more than one individual as actual producers, payment will be made to them jointly to a maximum of $200 for each such producer. In other words, if they have more than 400 acres and two people are in partnership on a joint permit they

would each get $200. If they had only 300 acres they would receive $150 each, in that particular case.
The second matter is in connection with cooperatives. Payment will be made to co-operatives based on a maximum of 200 for each active member of the co-operative and again to the extent of the total cultivated acres shown in the permit. If there are five people in the co-operative and they have 1,000 acres they get $200 apiece; if they have 500 acres they get $100 apiece.
The next matter is in connection with landlords. A large number of questions were raised last year as to whether they would get the payments, and there were complaints when they did not. I should like to make it clear that since the payment is made to the party shown as the actual producer in the wheat board permit, landlords are not eligible for payment unless they are listed as the actual operators of the land. The next point concerns the acreage eligible for payment. All acreage to a maximum of 200 acres which is shown in the wheat board delivery permit as being under wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax, cultivated forage crops, miscellaneous crops, summerfallow and new breaking is eligible for payment. This means, of course, that the only land which is not eligible is that which is natural pasture. There is one other point in this regard; it is the one I have just mentioned, but perhaps it should be put separately so that there may be no confusion. The acreage which is listed in the permit book as being uncultivated land or natural pasture is not eligible.
I trust this explanation will ensure that there is no such confusion with regard to these various points on this occasion as there was in regard to all these matters on the first occasion when acreage payments were made in 1958.
When I was introducing this estimate in 1958 and also in 1960 I referred to a table which gives the breakdown of specified acreage groups as shown by the wheat board delivery permits and I think it would be of advantage to members of the committee if I put this on the record of the house as I did in 1958. (Translation) :
That promise is probably one of those which the Prime Minister forgot to fulfil, and it is not the least, since it concerns 220,000 farmers in the three prairie provinces. Once again, the Prime Minister repudiates his promises to give parity and not charity to grain growers.
In 1960, when a similar vote was before the house, the Prime Minister, after having apologized for not being able to grant the deficiency payments asked by the wheat, oats and barley growers, said:
Deficiency payments applied to deliveries of grain would fail to help those producers most in need and if adopted would require very large subsidies from the treasury, which would inevitably lead to increased surpluses and would add further to the burden of financing the disposal of those surpluses.
And a little further on, the Prime Minister said:
As a result, our policy has consistently emphasized measures to attack the basic problems of agriculture; measures such as export assistance, crop insurance, a vastly improved and comprehensive agricultural credit policy, rural development, conservation and the like. We believe that the basic problems of Canadian agriculture will yield only to long range solutions.
Such was the Prime Minister's agricultural philosophy at that time. And now, in order to solve the problem, we have to take emergency measures as we did in 1958, 1960 and again this year, in other words, handouts, charity. No measure taken so far has given the results expected and the long range effects which were supposed to be felt.

The Crop Insurance Act would have played a suppletory part if the object of the legislation had been really to help the farmer, instead of being merely eyewash.
A few areas have been organized in the western provinces, but, in its application, the act did not reach as far as it should have, because it imposed too heavy a financial burden on the provincial governments.
Farmers in the east have a lot of sympathy for those of the west, and they proved it often last summer as well as in 1958 and 1960.
The fortunes of our farmers in the east are closely tied to those of their fellow farmers in the west, because it is from them that they get much of their supply of feed grain. Indeed, when agriculture is flourishing in the west, our whole economy is the better for it.
Mr. Chairman, the financial help given to farmers who suffered losses last summer will no doubt be appreciated, but, next spring, comes sowing time, it will not be enough to pay for the expenses they will have to incur in order to buy seed grain, gas and other items.
At the present time, most farmers have delivered the greater part of their grain; by next spring, they will have practically none left to bring in a cash income.
These circumstances will give rise to a serious problem where the farmer will be in for trouble if he cannot find ways of financing.
The regulations of the Farm Credit Corporation and the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act do not allow loans to be made to cover operating expenses. Of course, farmers may get a personal loan from the credit unions or the chartered banks but there again, only a small portion of them take advantage of such loans because they have no securities to offer.
I would therefore suggest that the government amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act in order to enable the corporation to grant short term loans as the Liberal party has often recommended and as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has also proposed in the brief submitted to the government four or five years ago.

I listened with a great deal of attention when the Acting Minister of Agriculture was introducing this item, and I appreciated the information and statistics he gave us.
On this occasion he engaged in very little extraneous argument but merely set forth the views of the government justifying this payment to producers in various categories. However, the first thing which strikes me in regard to the government's attitude is the long delay in making an announcement. For a great number of years farmers have been pressing for parity prices for agricultural products. In asking for parity prices they sought a set of prices related to costs of production. They did not in any way ask for handouts or charity.
One of the reasons so many members from the three prairie provinces sit on the government side of the house was the belief which producers in western Canada had in the Prime Minister, when he told them during the election campaign that there would be charity, not parity.
It is the other way around.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: He is always twisting something.

I think I have been around some of the members opposite a little too long. The Prime Minister promised parity not charity, but the farmers have waited a long time for parity prices. The principle of parity prices has not been applied to a single farm commodity since this government was elected.
Other measures have been brought in by the government to deal with prices of agricultural products, but in almost every instance the action taken by the government has meant lower support prices, less support, and a smaller guarantee than the farmers had previously. The government has only acted in regard to these payments after a great deal of pressure. Its first announcement that $1 per acre would be paid was made early in August, 1958, after the government had been returned to office, and after farm organizations had continued to press every strongly for parity prices and deficiency payments.
The payments brought forward at that time were made applicable to the 1958-59 crop year and paid on those permit books. Western farmers were dissatisfied with the action which was taken and hoped that in the future the government would do more. They were determined that the government should do no less than provide the $40 million which had been put forward in the estimates in August 1958. We waited during the year 1959 for an announcement by the
[The Deputy Chairman.]
government. None was forthcoming. No announcement of any payment was made during that year. After persistent pressure from agricultural organizations, after a delegation of more than a thousand farmers marched on Ottawa. After protracted correspondence with the government, an announcement was made on August 8, 1960 that a dollar an acre would again be paid on acreage up to a maximum of 200 acres and that this would be paid on the 1959-60 permit books. Thus, with the announcement on August 8 the farmers did receive $1 an acre in accordance with this formula for 1958-59. With the further announcement a dollar an acre was forthcoming on the 1959-60 crop.
Producers had reason to expect that last year, again, the government would make an announcement that it was paying a dollar an acre on the 1960-61 permit books. I asked the Prime Minister in the house last fall whether he intended to take this action but all we got was the brush-off.
The hon. member asked him in July, too.

I take it it was the Prime Minister,

though the Governor General reads it. And in the speech from the throne the following statement is made:
The drought in the prairie provinces during 1961 has resulted in severe losses . .. and you will be asked to provide assistance by means ot acreage payments to the farmers who have been affected.
Well, I hope the government does that. The announcement made today does not derive from that statement in the speech from the throne because, as hon. members will have seen, the statement in the speech from the throne says there will be acreage payments to the farmers who have been affected by the drought. All they are doing in this thing is to use the same old catch all, paying it to a farmer with 40 bushels an acre as well as to the man who had a zero yield. Either the Prime Minister does not watch very carefully the things he writes when he is supposed to be writing the speech from the throne or-and I hope this is correct-the thing we are dealing with today is not the policy forecast in the speech from the throne.
I say this because the provision before us today has absolutely nothing to do with drought-nothing whatsoever. This money is to be paid to grain producers, wheat producers, barley producers, oats producers and to the men who produce hay. It is paid to many men who produce livestock and sell no grain. It is paid to people who do not sell a bushel of grain. It has nothing whatever to do with drought. I suggest the farmers of western Canada will be looking to the Prime Minister to fulfil by way of legislation the undertaking announced in the speech from the throne, namely to bring in acreage payments to the farmers affected by drought. The farmers who have been so affected have put forward their case for acreage payments. That has nothing to do with this proposition whatsoever. The farm unions, by way of a policy statement submitted to the government, have asked for a $5 per acre payment to farmers who have experienced crop failure as defined in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, namely, a yield of less than 12 bushels per acre. They have asked for an acreage payment up to $1,000 for farmers who have suffered crop failure. I have a resolution on the order paper asking for similar action to be taken, asking that there be an expansion of the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act so that farmers who have experienced crop failure may receive compensation in a more adequate fashion. My resolution asks that the payment be increased and that the acreage on which the payment may be made should also be increased.
The announcement which was made today will be a great disappointment to western producers, because as far as western producers 26207-1-174
Supp ly-A griculture
are concerned it will be considered to represent just half as much as they felt they had a right to expect. The Prime Minister announced an acreage payment on the 1958-59 crop year and an acreage payment on the 1959-60 crop year. Now he has skipped a year. The announcement today is merely in respect of the 1961-62 crop year. The farmers will realize that they have been gypped by the omission of the crop year 1960-61. The Prime Minister says it is for the two-price system. In the speech from the throne he said it is for the drought. This has nothing to do with the two-price system, though that is what he said. Why did he not have it for the two-price system in 1960-61? What was wrong with paying it in that year? Why miss a year? At least we know why this one is being included. It is an election year.

On a question of privilege, the hon. member for Assiniboia has been making statements saying that the Prime Minister had said this, and had said that, without giving the committee any authority in support of those statements. He has not told us where those statements were reported or recorded and I should like to know where the hon. member gets his authority for attributing, for instance, the words "parity not charity". I should also like to know what is his authority for saying that when the Prime Minister came back from the west he said conditions were not as bad as he had thought.

I am disappointed that the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek should stand up and repudiate this promise made by the Prime Minister time and time again that we would get parity not charity. My authority for what the Prime Minister has been saying is the speech from the throne. He may say that the Governor General wrote it himself and did not ask for any advice, but with the words that were placed in the mouth of the Governor General the Prime Minister has said the acreage payment will be made to the farmers who have been affected by the drought.
Of course, this has not been done. This apparently is not going to be done. I should like to know from the gladiators from the prairies who sit on the government side of the chamber whether they think the farmers have a right to expect a payment for the 1960-61 crop year.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. You did not deal with the last point. The hon. member has not quoted any authority for what he has said; he is merely trying to misinterpret the point of order of the hon. member. He said he repudiated the

Supply-Agriculture
Prime Minister. There was no such suggestion. I think the point of order was well taken. The hon. member says he is quoting the words of the Prime Minister and I think it is perfectly in order for an hon. member to suggest that the hon. member who is quoting someone should give a reference of when and where such a statement was made.

Mr. Chairman, I do not mind these interruptions as long as you keep track of the time taken up by these interferences. It is interesting to note how widely the Prime Minister is being repudiated, and I suggest that when-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman.
There is another phony point of order being raised in the wings there.

The hon. member is interpreting my words as meaning that the Prime Minister has been repudiated. I am merely saying that the hon. member who is purporting to quote the Prime Minister should say when and where he was speaking. The hon. member says this is a phony point of order. Certainly if the objection taken to the last point of order was sound, this one is not. This one is ill-taken. I would ask the Chair to kindly direct the hon. member to give his reference and quit giving these phony references to mythical speeches.
If I may continue with my remarks that are causing so much consternation among the members on the government side of the chamber-
These misquotations always cause consternation.

The farmers of western Canada will be deeply disappointed that this government has omitted in the payments to them the crop year 1960-61. Of course, this is the way the Prime Minister works. The Prime Minister will not say on a given occasion the policy of the government with relation to acreage payments over a period of time. No, it is a hit or miss affair. He wants them to come begging. He wants to keep them on tenterhooks. He wants to have a carrot on the stick. He wants to feed them a little before the election and withdraw it after the election if he should be in that position.
I do not think this is the way either to treat the agricultural producers or the House of Commons. If we are to be dealing periodically with a measure to pay $1 an acre to western farmers under a certain formula, then I suggest the government should put forward this policy in legislative form and place it on the statute books so that the legislation is made in an equitable, regular manner and is not in this most unsatisfactory way of having an item in the estimates one year,
[Mr. Nugent. 1
missing a year and putting it in the estimates at some later time.
But the Prime Minister thinks in every field, apparently, as a politician. He has come to the conclusion that he can garner more votes by this slipshod method of dealing with a very important question. The Prime Minister would like western Canada to think that he is the only Prime Minister who has ever done anything for the grain producers. He would like them to think that his legislation has put more into the pockets of the grain producers than other legislation.
I have debated in this house for many years with former minsters of agriculture and trade and commerce, but there was one policy that was placed on the statute books in 1956 that I feel was a good one. That had to do with the national treasury paying the carrying charges on stocks of wheat held at the end of each crop year in excess of 178 million bushels.
This kind of payment is a regular one. This kind of payment is placed on the statute books. This kind of payment may not receive the same spectacular publicity because it is sure and it is certain. But I suggest it is a much better way of handling the business of this country than by the political method of the carrot on the stick, where you can have a nibble before the election and you are forgotten the year after the election.
In 1957-58 under this particular policy $33 million was paid to the grain producers of western Canada. In the next year, $40 million was paid and in the next year $38 million. In 1960-61, $42 million was paid, and for the present year it is estimated at $49 million.
Did you call it peanuts then?

Under this policy of paying money into the wheat board fund for storage on wheat that was held in excess of 178 million bushels the treasury has made over the years, I estimate, total payments of $202 million, as opposed to the $126 million that will be paid in the three years in which the $1 an acre has been paid.
I am not endeavouring to set one policy against the other on the basis of which policy is the better one, but I do say to this government that if their policy is $1 an acre, it should be in the statute books; it should be regularized. It should not be available only when the Prime Minister is in the right frame of mind and decides that this is the politically opportune time to bring forward this kind of payment.
The policy that is being put forward today has been put forward on the ground that it is a help to the small farmer. It is a help to some small farmers, but it is a help to

the big farmers. There is a ceiling on it of $200 payable to every farmer who has 200 acres or more in crop. But according to the figures put forward by the minister this morning it is only the small farmer who does not get the full benefit. According to the figures put forward by the minister this morning 20,000 farmers with 99 acres or less will get less than $200. Another 55,000 farmers with acreages of between 100 and 199 will get less than $200. So that about one third of the farmers on the prairies will get less than the $200 put forward in this proposal. Therefore it is not something that provides a minimum payment, a guaranteed basic, floor payment to the small farmers. Instead it is put forward on the basis of a payment to farmers, one third of whom will get less than the $200.
We are still looking forward to the government fulfilling its promises of bringing forth parity prices for agricultural products, and the argument in favour of something more being done is the tremendous increase in the farmer's cost of production over the years.
The 11-factor index for the farmer's cost of production stood at 170.4 in 1947. The last figures I have available show that the index today is 286 and it has gone up 27.5 points since 1957 when this government took office. It is the price cost squeeze resulting in higher and higher costs for farmers in western Canada that has created this demand for acreage payments, for deficiency payments, for income supports of one type and another. I can understand spokesman for agriculture from other parts of Canada saying "We want a payment like this" or "We want some other payment to equal this". This payment is made on the basis of acreage and farmers who produce in eastern Canada have acres just the same as have farmers producing in western Canada. This proposition is not put forward as a well defined policy. It is put forward on a temporary basis. It is not put forward with a formula attached that will be used year after year. I think it is a slipshod way of doing business that will be bound to create in the country much more resentment than would be the case if it were made. That would remove controversy on this question from parliament year after year.
This provision in itself is not nearly enough to meet the agricultural situation as we find it at this time. If the farmers of Canada, are to get a square deal I suggest that the government should provide a system of deficiency payments for grain. These deficiency payments should be based on a formula and they should be designed to give the farmer parity prices for his grain products. Second,
Supply-Agriculture
I would suggest that there should be a large expansion in prairie farm assistance payments that are made; that there should be an increase in the acreage on which payments can be made from 400 to 600 acres; that there should be a thorough overhaul of the government's crop insurance scheme; and that the federal government should bear a much larger share of the burden and should do more than merely agree to pay 20 per cent of the forecast premiums under this legislation.
Third, I would make this suggestion. If the government really wants to do something in a major way for small farmers, I would suggest that in addition to anything that is being done today the government should provide floor prices, and not this hocus-pocus of a national average that is in the agricultural prices stabilization legislation. I submit that the government should provide floor prices on hogs, eggs and poultry.
The farmers would not be asking for deficiency payments or acreage payments if they were getting parity prices. In recent months there has been a considerable improvement in the selling price for Canadian grain. As a matter of fact there would seem to be a real indication now that Canada, along with other nations of the world, may be able to negotiate a new international wheat agreement that will provide substantially higher prices. My fourth suggestion is this. In the present context of the international wheat situation I would think that the Canadian government should endeavour to have the international wheat agreement renegotiated with its target being an increase of 50 cents per bushel in the floor price and an increase of 50 cents per bushel in the ceiling price. This action would bring these prices more in line with the guaranteed prices that are obtained by United States grain producers and would be reasonably in line, I feel, with the upward pressure on wheat prices throughout the world at this time.
As a fifth point I would suggest that at this session the government should amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act so as to make it permanent legislation. I suggest that the government should not have it contain a date at which it terminates unless it is otherwise extended but should make it permanent legislation, in order to reassure the producers of western Canada that the government will maintain the Canadian wheat board.
As a sixth point, I would suggest the government should increase the scope and the powers of the Canadian wheat board and that this government should cease weakening the Canadian wheat board by taking feed

Supp ly-A griculture
grains sold to feed mills from under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board. The jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board over feed grains should be restored. The Canadian wheat board legislation should apply to rye and flax.
As point number seven I would suggest that, in addition to window dressing and printing pamphlets, the government should take some action in connection with A.R.D.A., the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, should sign an agreement with the provinces in order to obtain for livestock producers-

speechtext: Order. I think I have been very charitable in allowing these planks to be placed before the committee in respect of all other fields of agriculture except the one in the item under consideration. I would ask the hon. member who has the floor and whose time expires in one minute or so, to hearken back to the subject under consideration.
I would hope, in view of your ruling, that would mean that I have some further time because of the interruptions.
Keep in order and you will not be interrupted.

To conclude, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say this. As far as the livestock producers are concerned, which this $1 an acre will help in exactly the same way as it will help the grain producers, one of the things necessary for the government to do in order to improve their situation is to provide them with access to grazing, by an increase in community pastures and by redevelopment of the kind the government has been talking about.
As an eighth alternative or addition to the things that are now being done, I would suggest that the government should protect the long gains of western producers in many fields. This measure will be of some assistance because $200 is better than nothing. However, the $200 payment will scarcely pay for the 3 per cent increase announced a few weeks ago in the prices of farm machinery charged by the International Harvester Company. Welcome as it is, this $200 will in no way compensate the farmer for the increased costs that will follow if this government and future governments were foolish enough to allow the suggestion of the royal commission on transportation to go forward and abandon most of the railway lines in western Canada, thereby increasing the cost of marketing grain by an enormous amount.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that this item is welcome. It is better than nothing. Previously I had called it peanuts in relation

to farm costs. The bag that contains the peanuts is smaller for the small farmer than for the larger farmer. This is small compensation for the huge increase in the cost of farming and the cost of production. I suggest that the very minimum the Prime Minister should do is to make this payment on the 1960-61 crop year as well as in the present year and to make this legislation permanent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
For the third time in a row now, Mr. Chairman, we have heard this same speech from the hon. member for Assiniboia in which he uses this opportunity to lay down the various shaky planks in his election platform. He uses this as an opportunity to make his one agricultural speech in the session and to create the impression that he is doing his bit here in the House of Commons in order to help the farmers he represents.
I think perhaps we can best deal with the contribution he has just made by reading an item which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post of October 20, when the opposition in the legislature were criticizing the government for the action during the drought. It reads as follows:
Existing government policies of help to farmers had made it unnecessary to call a special session of the legislature to deal with the 1961 farm crisis, provincial treasurer Woodrow Lloyd said Thursday.
So his colleagues in the province of Saskatchewan do not agree with him when he says that conditions in the drought areas of Saskatchewan were so severe that additional assistance must be provided by the government. There is an article in the same edition of the Regina Leader-Post quoting Mr. Nollet, the provincial minister of agriculture, to this effect:
-the government had done everything possible to help the farmers both to fight grasshoppers and to help overcome the effects of the drought.. . He charged that the Liberals only wanted to stir up a fuss in the face of a calamity to try to get people to believe them. He said it was "the poorest kind of political practice that could ever be followed, since it put a very low level of intelligence on the people of the province."
That is precisely what the hon. member for Assiniboia is attempting to do today. His statement that price supports have been lower since the present government took office is completely false. In most cases price supports have been raised and a larger number of farm commodities have been brought under support. Surely the hon. member does not expect he is going to get anyone to believe that his statement that price supports have been lowered is the truth. The hon. member went to some length to be critical of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture in their efforts to do something to help the farmers of Canada. I think his criticism can be effectively refuted by an article that

appeared in the December issue of The Country Guide. As everyone knows, The Country Guide is a very objective and independent paper. The title of the editorial is, "Hurrah for Mr. Hamilton", and it has this to say, in part:
But setting the drought problem aside for the time being, it should be recognized that there have been a number of positive steps forward and several important breakthroughs in the field of farm policy in the past year.
The editorial goes on to say:
The Hon. Alvin Hamilton has held this post in the federal cabinet for just over a year now. To our way of thinking, he is proving to be an excellent minister of agriculture.
I do not want to trespass on the rules of the house, Mr. Chairman, but I feel that a number of the charges that were made by the hon. member when he digressed from the item in question must be answered. I think I should have the same leeway in replying to those accusations as he had in making them. The excerpt I now wish to read is in answer to the criticism of the hon. member that the Department of Agriculture is carrying on too much publicity. This is what The Country Guide has to say about the matter:
He has made a special effort to explain the problems of agriculture to the consuming public in order to gain understanding and support for needed agricultural policies. He has launched an effective publicity campaign on his departmental programs to ensure that farm people will be fully familiar with how to make the best of the opportunities and assistance they provide.
The editorial goes on to say:
First, the Canada Department of Agriculture must change its emphasis from the production or supply side to the demand side of the market. Second, ways must be found for the federal government to work in greater harmony and co-operation with the provinces on agricultural programs.
That is precisely what the minister is doing.
Third, agriculture must work in greater co-operation with the other resource industries in Canada. Each of these three approaches is commendable.
In conclusion this statement is made:
A great many things remain to be done.
We are the first ones to admit that the problems of agriculture as well as the problems of any other industry in this country are never completely solved.
However, his willingness to act on any valid complaint or promising proposal, his boundless energy and enthusiasm, his sound philosophy and imaginative approach to the problems of today and tomorrow, are not only commendable characteristics, but provide hope for agriculture that has been sadly lacking in recent years. May his efforts in 1962 be as rewarding for agriculture as they have been in the year that is about to close.
Contrary to what the hon. member has been saying, these are the views of the farm
Supply-Agriculture
organizations. This is what they are saying about the government and the Minister of Agriculture. I wish to refer to another item that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, I believe it is, of January 13. It has reference to a statement made by Mr. S. E. Ransom, president of the Manitoba federation of agriculture, and is in these words:
Canadian agriculture has about reached the limit of support and intervention it can expect from governments, S. E. Ransom, Manitoba federation of agriculture president, said in Winnipeg Friday .. . He cited the recent passing of the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act as a case in point, and called for steps to be adopted along the same lines whereby farmers and farm groups could do something constructive to get themselves out of the dilemma of high cost, low return production.
The farmers themselves recognize what the government is doing to try to assist them. They are organizing in an effort to co-operate with the government, as the minister has pointed out on so many occasions and, as is stated in the editorial in The Country Guide, the minister is working for greater cooperation between farm organizations and the federal and provincial governments and related industries. We feel that this is an effective way in which the problems of agriculture can be met, first of all by government legislation designed to assist the farmers to help themselves; second, by greater cooperation and, third, by government policies designed to relieve some of the distress that exists because of low income and low yields.
No one on this side of the house has ever tried to create the impression that acreage payments are intended to be the answer to the agricultural problem. They are a measure designed to offset the effects of low income as a result of drought last year. They are intended to assist farmers, particularly those in the lower income range, to maintain their farming operations until they have had an opportunity to take advantage of the different pieces of legislation and types of assistance available to them under this government.
The hon. member for Assiniboia has criticized several of them but he is critical in the same way that Mr. Nollet has accused the opposition in the provincial legislature of being critical. Crop insurance has not been fully applied across the country but I have no doubt that it will be. The reaction in the province of Manitoba because of the drought is an indication that there is going to be a greater signing up of farmers under the crop insurance legislation than ever before because after the drought last year they realized what crop insurance could do for them.
The efforts that the Minister of Agriculture has made to get rid of our wheat and, indeed, the efforts of the Minister of Finance, have

Supply-Agriculture
resulted in approximately a 20 cent increase in the price of wheat. Yet the hon. member for Assiniboia has the audacity to stand up here and say that prices have been reduced, that prices are going down and that there is less support. I challenge him to show me v/here price supports have been lowered on any commodity in this country, particularly in the past few years. I challenge him to go to the people of his constituency and, indeed, to the western provinces generally and spread the same type of claptrap that he spread this afternoon and try to get away with it.

Before the parliamentary secretary sits down I should like to ask him a question. Is he aware that in recent months many producers in western Canada have been selling eggs at 15 to 20 cents a dozen, and does he think that is an adequate support price?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As the hon. member well knows the price support policy on eggs is based on the national average.
That is the trouble; that is what I said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: At the end of the year, if the price is below the level that is set by the stabilization board, the farmers will be compensated and the hon. member knows that full well.
But there is no floor price.

I am sure we all regret that the Minister of Agriculture, because of illness, is not in his seat and, on that account, is not able to introduce this measure, initiated today by the former minister of agriculture, the present Minister of National Defence. I am sure, too, that on the occasion when we first discuss a matter concerning agriculture, we noted with considerable regret the recent death of a former minister of agriculture, the late Right Hon. J. Gardiner. Mr. Gardiner, regardless of whether or not one agreed with him, was deserving of high tribute from the Prime Minister, who led the nation in expressing deep sorrow at the passing of one who had contributed so much to Canada and to agriculture. As a former colleague, I take this occasion to express in this house my own inadequate but sincere tribute to a great minister of agriculture, one who did so much for western Canada and who was one of the great parliamentarians of this period in Canada.
This measure, Mr. Chairman, was announced not in parliament but on the occasion of a visit by the Prime Minister to his constituency last fall. It was an announcement made at a time when I believe the Minister of Agriculture was in the province

of Saskatchewan, meeting, at the same time, representatives of certain farm groups. The Calgary Albertan observes that the Prime Minister made his announcement of this acreage assistance following the pattern of the two previous occasions when this method was used, to constituents of his in a theatre that had seats for 800 but where only 700 people were in attendance. In any event, the Prime Minister, of course, had a right to choose this way of making the announcement, but it is an announcement that came under circumstances that at least must be questioned.
As late as last July, the hon. member for Assiniboia had asked a question of the Prime Minister in this house, and questions were put by other members of the opposition in the month of September last, as to when the house might be expected to deal with the legislation that had been forecast in news stories some time in the month of July. As I say, however, it was only last fall that the Prime Minister gave a positive announcement of the government program. When the Prime Minister did make the announcement I suppose that one would regard the observations of Mr. Rudy Usick, the president of the Manitoba farmers union, as typical of the complaints that were registered against the inadequacy of the particular program. Mr. Rudy Usick associated with his complaint the fact that since the first acreage covered the crop year from August 1, 1958 to July 31,
1959,	the second covered the calendar year
1960,	and the third covered the crop year August 1, 1961 to July 31, 1962, the farmers had been done out of payments for five months of 1959 and seven months of 1961.
This point was made by the hon. member for Assiniboia and has not been replied to by the parliamentary secretary who has just taken his seat. One of the most amazing things about this program is, as the hon. member for Assiniboia has said, that this is not a fulfilment of the promise made by the government and notably by the Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition and later during the course of the federal election. At that time, he indicated to the people of Canada what his government would do to try and remedy the situation that confronted Canadian agriculture. The hon. member for Assiniboia and my colleague, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska referred to the promises made by the Prime Minister. We were not going to have mere handouts such as this, good as it is, inadequate as it is, we were going to have a comprehensive program; parity not charity. When that statement was made, hon. gentlemen opposite asked, what was the source, what was the authority for saying that the Prime Minister

had ever said that parity not charity would be the objective of his party when it constituted the government of this country.
No source was given for the statement. Let me remind hon. gentlemen that there will be found at page 2021 of Hansard for March 12, 1956 these words spoken by the Prime Minister:
The squeeze which the farmer suffers results from the disparity in the relationship between the prices of farm products and the prices the farmer has to pay. When they are in proper relationship parity is established, and it is parity that the farm organizations across this country are asking for today. Not charity but parity.
There is my reply which the hon. member for Assiniboia did not give to the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. Hon. gentlemen will also find, at page 2026 of Hansard for March 12, 1956, that the Prime Minister expressed this objective in the form of an amendment which he moved. This amendment reads as follows:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.
There is the authority in so far as the records of this house are concerned. If any more proof is required, I ask my hon. friend to look at what the Prime Minister said in Toronto in his opening speech of the campaign on April 25, 1957; I ask them to read what he said as recorded in the Winnipeg Free Press on April 26 and likewise to look at what was reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail, indicating that the Prime Minister said on the hustings precisely what he has said in this house that what he was going to give the farmers was not $1 per acre with a maximum of $200, not charity but parity. This was the assurance given by the Prime Minister, who is in the house today, to the farmers of Canada. What do we have now? We have for a third time-
We have $1.90 a bushel wheat.

-something altogether different from the promised comprehensive program based upon a continuing body of principles as envisaged by the Prime Minister at that time. Let the government, the Acting Minister of Agriculture and the parliamentary secretary not seek to indicate that by coming forward with this measure they are fulfilling their promises. The Prime Minister boasts of having fulfilled almost all of his promises. Well, we all know the extent to which there has been any fulfilment, and if there is one area where there has been 26207-1-18
Supply-Agriculture
no implementation of promises made by the Prime Minister, it is in the field of agriculture.
Nonsense.
This particular program is now brought forward at a late date in spite of assertions and hints as to what was going to be done, assertions made no later than last summer.
That is just plain tommyrot.

Hon. gentlemen are indicating that they do not like my remarks. They do not like to be reminded that the farmers were promised a new earth. They do not like to be told that if there is one section of the Canadian electorate that is disappointed with the government it is the farmers of Canada. They do not like this.
That is all hogwash.

That is why we are hearing these sitting contributions to the debate, by way of a continuous effort on the part of those who sit behind the Prime Minister to hinder those in this party who are determined to expose the government once again in this session, as it deserves to be exposed, because of the inept way in which it is conducting the affairs of the country.
You know so much about agriculture that you cannot even talk sense about it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Orda\

We who come from eastern Canada recognize that the farmers of our country, particularly those in western Canada, are facing great problems but we recognize it is our duty not to view those problems sectionally but in the light of constructive solutions.
Like the Liberals did.

We give support to this measure, but at the same time we say to the government there are other sections of agriculture, for instance, the farmers in the township of Sandwich East in my own riding, in the community of Tecumseh, who last year suffered crop losses for which the government, in spite of representations, have not agreed to make any compensation. What we do for the western farmers, and what we should do for the eastern farmers, is to bring in measures which will apply equally to all sections of Canadian agriculture.
Why was this program not brought forward a long time ago? Why was it not brought forward last summer when the house was in session? Why was it not brought forward in the month of September when the house was

Supp ly-A griculture
in session? It was because at that time the Prime Minister had not decided on calling a general election. It is brought forward now because he realizes his strength has disappeared in western Canada. Because of that he seeks by this measure to recover his lost popularity and prestige, lost even in Prince Albert. I say the measure should have been brought forward at least last summer. I do not say that it represents all that should have been done but, if this is all the government is prepared to do to meet the situation facing the farmers of Canada, then it should have been introduced at a time when the farmers would not have lost five months of the crop year.
What is the explanation given by the government with regard to this matter? We have a most amazing situation. At the end of November, 1961, the Minister of Agriculture was asked if the government was going to bring forward the much-mooted acreage assistance plan. Here is what he said as reported in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix on November 29, 1961. It is headed:
Hamilton holds out promise of payments on acreage plan.
This is a statement I now read, not on the hustings but on the floor of parliament where we all have a responsibility in the light of our acknowledged recognition of what is the function and obligation of parliament in the voting of public money. At the time he made the statement no money at all had been voted. Parliament had not dealt with this matter. We are dealing with it now for the first time this session, and yet the Minister of Agriculture sought to convey to the farmers in western Canada that the government had authority to pay out this money. Listen to the statement which the minister made:
It's not a matter of money, but machines.
Today Hon. Alvin Hamilton, home from grainselling trips which have taken him half way around the world, said that there would be no farm acreage payments in this calendar year. He did not attribute this to lack of federal dollars but said that the cheque machines required to roll out the barrels of money were busy with other financial details.
The agricultural minister did say the federal government had not abandoned the principle of acreage payments to western farmers.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that statement of the Minister of Agriculture was an inaccurate statement. The statement as reported, is an inaccurate statement.
As reported.

The reason the money was not paid out in November, or earlier, was because the government had not come to parliament and asked it to vote the necessary assistance to the farmers of western Canada. That was the reason, and let the

western members who sit in the house today write to their constituents and tell them the Minister of Agriculture was wrong, wholly wrong, in saying that the reason this money had not been paid out earlier was because the machinery for issuing cheques had broken down.
The Prime Minister laughs, but I ask him to listen to another statement made by his Minister of Agriculture, which I take from the Winnipeg Free Press of December 1, 1961. The headline is:
Farmers will get paid before Yule.
And the article states:
Mr. Hamilton said acreage payments still are under consideration by the government but it will be technically impossible to make acreage payments this year because cheque machines are being used for the oats and barley pools and the interim wheat payment.
What is wrong with that?

It is an untrue statement. That is what is wrong with it. The reason the cheques were not paid out was not because of faulty machinery in issuing them but because the government did not come to parliament and ask for authority to vote the moneys required to make these acreage payments. That is the reason that should have been given to the farmers of western Canada at that time, but it was not done. The Prime Minister made his announcement at Prince Albert and said nothing about the breakdown of machinery for the issuing of cheques. He made a forthright statement to which no exception could be taken in its accuracy of terms, but just a few days previously the Minister of Agriculture had created the impression that the money was then available, that it would be paid out to the farmers of western Canada and that the only reason for it not being paid out was because the system for issuing cheques had broken down.
Nobody said it had broken down.
My hon. friend must not have been listening with great attention when he says nobody said it had broken down. That is what the Minister of Agriculture did say.
Quote him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Verbatim.
This was the report.
You are just backing down now.

This vote represents an ad hoc way of dealing with a particular situation. There is no government policy involved in the pattern of this program. This is a single item, a palliative designed to give relief. It will give relief to an extent, but not to the extent envisaged by the kind of all-embracing statement made by the Prime Minister in his statement of agricultural intentions in the house on August 8 last year.
This is not a program based upon a continuing policy. This is not a grant related to the cost of production or to prices. The Prime Minister said that the agricultural policy of this government would be one which would take into account the cost-price squeeze and the disparity of farm prices in relation to the income of other classes in the community. He said it would be a program related to the cost of production and the revenue which farmers receive for the sale of their products. This program, good in so far as it goes, in no way meets the extravagant, comprehensive assurances given to the people of Canada by the Prime Minister.
As I mentioned a moment ago, it certainly is not what he said on March 12, 1956 in this house. It certainly is not a grant by way of deficiency payments. It certainly is not a grant made under the Agricultural Stabilization Act of which the Acting Minister of Agriculture claims authorship. It has no relation to the general problem of agriculture and no relation whatever to the general economic situation facing the farmers of Canada. It is obviously a compromise between the demands made by certain western ministers in the cabinet and the stand taken by the Minister of Finance who apparently day by day increasingly resists the demands made by his colleagues for further expenditures of public money.

I wonder whether the hon. member is aware that the reason why wheat, oats and barley are not covered by the stabilization act is because of the request made to that effect by organized farmers in the west?

Quite. I am not saying that is not the case. I am saying that this particular program calling for expenditure of $40 million based on the payment of $1 assistance per acre up to 200 acres is not related to the Agricultural Stabilization Act. It does not involve the principle of deficiency payments and it can in no way be represented as part of the over-all program envisaged by the Prime Minister when he spoke in this house in 1956 or when he spoke in this house in August of last year at which time he outlined the government's 26207-1-184

agricultural policy. I repeat that the Prime Minister and his supporters cannot claim that by this particular program they are satisfying the promises which were made to hundreds of Canadian western farmers.

I sincerely hope that is the case, but, as I have stated, this provision does not meet the objectives of the government's declared farm policy as announced by the Prime Minister. It does not meet the assurances given to a thousand western farmers when they descended on Ottawa two years ago to demand that this government implement its agricultural policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Nobody takes your interpretation.
Well, when the hon. gentleman and his colleagues decide, as I hope they will decide soon, to face the Canadian people they will see whether or not their policy satisfies the electorate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is exactly right.

This policy is an off and on policy. We are not able to say now whether it is going to be a permanent feature of the actions of the government of Canada. Let the Minister of Agriculture say now that if he were entrusted with the responsibility of government next year, something which I doubt very much, his government would embark once again on this particular program of assistance on an acreage basis. Let him say that, and we would then have some indication of whether there is a semblance of agricultural policy.
The most serious objection to this program is that it represents a stopgap handout with no precise relationship to the entire needs of the farm economy or to the needs of individual farmers. If the acting minister were able to tell us now that the provinces were heartily accepting the crop insurance scheme which was introduced two years ago, then he would be able to talk about something in the nature of a comprehensive policy, even though that would not be a realization of the promise that what the farmers were going to get would be parity not charity. That is the kind of thing to which this government must address itself if it wishes to demonstrate it is fulfilling its obligations to the farmers of western Canada.
We have the amazing situation of the Prime Minister announcing a policy in the province of Saskatchewan to his own constituents at a time when the Minister of Agriculture was in that province-at a time when the Minister of Agriculture gave the impression,

Supply-Agriculture
created undoubtedly by implication, that the government had authority to provide for this program. The Prime Minister, taking advantage of a visit to his constituency and speaking in a theatre in Prince Albert which was not filled, said: "We propose to embark once again on a program of acreage assistance". I say that for one minister of the crown to give the impression that the government had already embarked on such a policy and that parliament had already voted the money is a statement which calls for comment and reply by the Acting Minister of Agriculture, because it represents a base inaccuracy. This is a charitable way of dealing with that statement.
But this incident, of course, is only one further example of the way in which the government approaches these problems. The government seeks to take advantage of situations so that it can get the most dramatic effect for political and propaganda purposes. No one demonstrates this more clearly than the Minister of Agriculture in the program called A.R.D.A.

a program which is not designed to meet the current situation, a program in connection with which, as the hon. member for Assiniboia has pointed out, not one project has been realized in co-operation with the provinces under arrangements provided for in the act. The Minister of Agriculture goes all over this country speaking of A.R.D.A. as though it represented the most fundamental approach ever made to solving the problems of Canadian agriculture.
Hear, hear.

I have no doubt that in the long run it will help Canadian agriculture but let hon. gentlemen not forget that that program in connection with which thousands of pamphlets have been issued was conceived by the previous government as a result of studies made by it in the upper house. The committee on land use under the chairmanship of Senator Power provided the basis for the legislation which was passed in this chamber, in connection with which the Minister of Agriculture goes from one end of Canada to the other, concealing his failure to implement promises which have been made, by representing A.R.D.A. as a charter for agriculture. Not one thing has been done under A.R.D.A. I ask the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, who is now in his seat, to give me one project under that act that has been signed by the federal government-

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to speak in support of quick passage of the supplementary estimates now before us. I think it is very useful to have these supplementary estimates on one sheet. I am particularly interested in item No. 611, a vote of $42 million for acreage payments to western grain producers, and item No. 614, a vote for $40,090,000 for the federal share in the winter works program. I know we are not discussing item 614, but I think having the two together on the one page indicates the government's concern for equal treatment for all segments of the economy.
The $42 million in acreage payments will help bolster the income of western farmers, and the $40,090,000 to pay half the labour costs for municipal works will add to the income of another group of workers. Having the two of them together certainly emphasizes the government's concern for all segments of the economy.
I wish to thank the Acting Minister of Agriculture for the full outline he gave of acreage payments in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, who is ill.
Mr. Chairman, you allowed opposition speakers to wander considerably in their remarks on this item.
Oh, oh.

I hope to keep right to the one point except I think I should answer to a certain extent some of the statements

they made. I deal with one particularly. I think the hon. member for Assiniboia will be fair and say that the crop was better than was first expected. If he will go through some of the reports of the wheat pool he will see that the crop index was up three points, one time, and so many points, another time, and we got more than a half crop-
Why did the Prime Minister not come to southern Saskatchewan instead of wandering all over the rest of the country?
He came to southern Saskatchewan.
He did not.
Southern Saskatchewan is not all in your area. It is in my area too.
He was not there during the crop failure.
He was in my area.
Then he should have learned something.

He was in my area and he saw something. I think the hon. member for Assiniboia will admit that the reports of the wheat pool show that the index went up by so many points and we did have more than a half crop. This was after we heard reports that there would be no crop at all in the country. I know that my own crop was much better than I had expected when I heard some of the dismal reports that the hon. member made. Also, the hon. member for Assiniboia made no reference at all to P.F.A.A., under which $50 million is being distributed. Many of the farmers who had poor crops are getting $800 cheques. That is partly due to the amendments that we brought in when we came into office.
The same rates were in effect when you were not in office.
They were not.
They were.

The whole thing was completely changed. If the hon. member will also refer to the last wheat board report he will see that already wheat exports for this year are more than 150 million bushels; already in four months more than half of the 10 year average for a whole year when the Liberal government was in power. In addition the price of wheat is now nearly 20 cents more than it was a year ago. I just draw this to the attention of hon. members. I know I should speak on the main item before us.
When I left home to attend this session of parliament I promised farming groups that I

would press for early action in regard to acreage payments. They had asked me to do this.

The reason we did not pay it last year was because you shouted "peanuts" and we had a great job trying to sell it again to the government.
Oh, oh. Forty seven members from the prairies and they cannot get anything done. Oh, oh, oh, what a joke.

The hon. member for Assiniboia indicated that farmers did not appreciate these acreage payments. I have received many letters from farm constituents supporting acreage payments. I do not wish to take the time of this committee by referring to them all, but I should like to quote a few excerpts from some of these letters. Here is one from Cymric:
With regard to the $200 acreage payment, I would sooner see this than to have the deficiency payments.

The letter is from H. J. Hilder-man.

With regard to the $200 acreage payment, I would sooner see this than to have the deficiency payments.

If the hon. member wants the names of all those who have written me, I have here another letter from Mr. Klenk of Imperial:
I sure favour the acreage payment over the extra payment on a specified number of bushels at the elevator, as it sure helps the farmer who has no bushels to sell.
Not so much when you miss a year, though.
It was on your account that we missed a year.
That is ridiculous.

There is another letter from George A. McDougall of Craven:
I am very much in favour of such assistance in preference to the deficiency payment. Being in the small farmer category myself, perhaps that is partly the reason but it seems by far the fairest way.
I hope the hon. member for Assiniboia heard that one.
Yes, but you should not have missed that year.
It was your fault that we did.
Oh, pay it now.
Keep quiet.

I am a three quarters section farmer and I think the acreage payment method will help more farmers than deficiency payments.
The letters should be tabled.

No opposition; we want it doubled.
I do not think the farmers of the west will take very kindly to what they have had to say.
