pay for the year that has been missed. Let us double it and then it will go through very quickly.

Then you will ask that
it be tripled.
Mr. Chairman, I mentioned nobody in particular and it is very interesting to see hon. members' reaction. If the cap fits certain hon. members, they can wear it.
Smearing John, eh?
I have not heard the hon. member for Assiniboia holler "peanuts" this year. I am very glad of that.
I rise on a point of order. I referred to peanuts. I said that the trouble this year was that the peanuts for the small farmer are in a smaller bag than those for the big farmer.
I suppose the hon. member indicates that he is not going to vote for this item. I am anxious to see what he does in this regard.
He wants the $200.
I will vote for it.

Several days ago he rose in his place in the house and actually asked for acreage payments. This was after the government had already heard from western supporters and had decided that acreage payments should be made this year.
Wrong again.

I suppose now the hon. member for Assiniboia will assert that it was his very belated request that resulted in these payments. This procedure will be following his usual practice. I believe on one other occasion he asserted that he or his party was responsible for a large sale of grain to Poland after the government had completed the deal.
That is not true. It was before they completed the deal.
Anyway, he asserted that he did it.
I met the delegation and we cooperated with the government.

On behalf of the constituents of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, I wish to thank the Prime Minister and the government for accepting our suggestions of this form of adding to the farm income. It will be a help not only to farm constituents but also to the whole economy. In this connection I refer to a news report which appeared in the Moose

Jaw Times-Herald dated March 15, 1961. I should like to refer briefly to it. The headline reads:
All Acreage Payments now in Farmers Hands- $3,801,000 Extra in Area.
Then there was an editorial in the Times-Herald which was headed "Acreage Payment Plan is Best for Farmers". The first two paragraphs of the news item read as follows:
It is estimated some $3,801,000 has been poured into the coffers of farmers living in the Moose Jaw trading area, from federal government acreage payments.
W. L. Burbank, secretary of the rural municipality of Moose Jaw, said today the extra flow of money from outside is hound to prosper the economy of this city.
The secretary of the municipality estimated that 95 per cent of this $3,801,000 would be spent in the local trading area. In Saskatchewan as a whole more than 106,000 grain growers received $19,732,906.
I should like to draw to the attention of the hon. member for Assiniboia the fact that this amount is certainly not peanuts.
I gave these figures in order to indicate the value of these payments at this time of the year when farmers are making plans for spring operations. I know western farmers are beginning to understand that acreage payments are actually along the lines of the two-price system they have been advocating for many years. Other groups in Canada's economy are also beginning to realize that the $42 million which this committee is asked to vote really means that the price for wheat sold for human consumption in Canada is in line with the price of products the farmer buys in Canada.
The money for this acreage payment comes out of the federal treasury. Western members appreciate the help given by the eastern members in getting this supplementary estimate before the committee. It was not an easy thing to do after the way in which earlier acreage payments were ridiculed by certain members of the opposition and even by some farm leaders.
Western farmers appreciate this government action, as was shown by the letters I read. Responsible farm leaders have indicated that they welcome the payments. As I say, even the hon. member for Assiniboia does not come right out and say that they are peanuts. Hence, Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister who first announced the government's intention should feel that the efforts of his government are fully appreciated. It is to be regretted that the Minister of Agriculture has been confined to his home for a few days, owing to the tremendous
Supply-Agriculture
efforts he has made in the past year in selling Canadian wheat and tackling other farm problems.
Does the hon. member not think that the weather had something to do with his cold?
For all these efforts on behalf of agriculture the farmers will thank the Minister of Agriculture, and the Prime Minister and his government, on election day.

I am very pleased to be given this opportunity to take part in the discussion of the estimates that are before the committee at the present time. This is now the third time that acreage payments will have been distributed to the western farmers. The amount will be another $42 million this year. The payments are similar to the ones that were distributed in 1958 and 1960. I remember very well the discussion that took place here in this House of Commons in 1958 when these estimates were presented to the house for approval. I also remember very well the remarks of the opposition and in particular those of our friend from Saskatchewan who at that time said they were peanuts. Those were the expressions that were used when these estimates were before the house. I must say that $42 million are not peanuts to the farmers of the three western provinces.
It is $1 an acre and that is peanuts.

The amount is equal to the amount the farmers would have received if we had had a two-price system, namely about $45 million. We are well aware of the fact that the government gave this assistance in lieu of the two-price system. They were not in a position to subsidize our grain at the time they gave it. I refer to grain that would be exported to the United States and other countries. I can recall very well the response of the fanners in my constituency to this $42 million. In my own community the payment amounted approximately to $30,000 a year. I have lived in this community for 30 years and this is the first time it has ever received $30,000 from the federal government.
I made it a point to ascertain where these acreage payment cheques were cashed and what they were used for. Cheques totalling the approximate value of $8,000 to $10,000 were cashed at our oil and gas station where the farmers paid for their oil and gas for the year in which it was received, namely 1958. Another $8,000 or $10,000 of them I found were cashed in our rural municipalities where the farmers paid their taxes for that year. Another $8,000 or $10,000 of them were cashed at the various stores in the community.

Surely this $30,000 these people were able to get in that community meant something to them. Is it any wonder that these farmers in the west-and I stress the words "in the west"-are now so appreciative of what the federal government has done for them and that the slogan in the country is now "Canada needs Diefenbaker"; and I would say that the west needs Diefenbaker.
They surely can have him.
They want the dollar an acre.
Other hon. members have had their say, Mr. Chairman. I have the floor and I should like to proceed.
Are you in favour of the payment for 1960-61? That is the question.

They know what the federal government has done. They also know that for years, when they sent down here and filled the treasury benches with members of the chief opposition party, they never received anything. They have received more in five years from this government than they ever did during the 25 years that the former government was in power.
I wonder whether I might ask the hon. member a question.
When I am through with my speech.
Is the hon. member in favour-

When I am through with my speech. The people in the west are satisfied with what the government has done. Five years ago they sent 47 members to this house. The people have seen the results and that is why the people of western Canada are saying that Canada needs Diefenbaker. For many years the people of Saskatchewan asked for the South Saskatchewan river project but only when the Prime Minister was elected as head of the government and 47 Conservative members were sent here from Saskatchewan and the other two western provinces was this objective realized.
Take the case of the people of Alberta. For 40 years they asked for the Pine Point railway but only when they sent a full slate of Conservative members to Ottawa did they get the Pine Point railway. For 20 years the people of Peace River sent Mr. Solon Low here. He was in the opposition and all he did was whine. He never did get the Pine Point railway for Alberta. Only when the present member for Peace River was sent here along with the Prime Minister did the people of that region get the Pine Point railway which is now under construction.
That is a dirty attack on a man who is not here to defend himself.

The people of Alberta, the people of Saskatchewan, the people of all three prairie provinces know that if they want to receive attention from the federal government they must send members here who are members of the party of the Prime Minister which is now in power.
You want a dictatorship of one party. You are not satisfied with 47 out of 48. You want a one party dictatorship.

The myth that we need a strong opposition has been killed in the west. The people know now that if they want to get results they must elect the present Prime Minister and give him the necessary support in the house.
A one-party dictatorship?

The hon. member for Assiniboia is not really appreciative of what we have done. Since 1945 he has done nothing but whine and wail to no avail, but now we have finally reached our objective and the west is getting the attention it needed because the people there elected the Prime Minister and gave him 47 members.

Mr. Chairman, as the representative of one of Manitoba's rural ridings I should like to comment briefly on this item dealing with acreage payments. First, I should like to express appreciation on behalf of those whom I represent of the fact that these payments are being considered as soon as possible after the convening parliament. I feel sure that the government's decision to make the payments available at this time will be welcomed by all western farmers, particularly because of the severe drought experienced last summer.
The payment of $1 an acre on the cultivated acreage of each farmer up to a maximum of $200, while not a large amount to each individual farmer in relation to what he would ordinarily expect as net income in a good year, is certainly not regarded by the farmers of my area as peanuts, as it was described by the hon. member for Assiniboia. As found at page 4348 of Hansard for August 30, 1958, the hon. member enlarged on that description. In speaking about acreage payments at that time the Leader of the Opposition said:
I have no doubt that when my hon. friend from Assiniboia gets up immediately after I conclude he will call it peanuts.
At that point the hon. member for Assiniboia interjected the following:
I did that a couple of days ago. I shall call it a pittance today.

As a matter of fact, it adds up to a considerable amount of benefit to our rural communities and assists not only the farmers but also those who provide goods and services to our farm people. Statistics show that farm gross income across the nation is making a steady recovery in relation to the income enjoyed by other segments of our economy. But statistics do not reach down to the individuals who have suffered grievous losses owing to the drought. This fact was recognized by the government and the Minister of Agriculture early last summer. At that time steps were taken to assure supplies of feed and to provide the necessary protection against serious income loss through forced selling of our cattle.
The result of the government's action is, of course, well known. With the fullest co-operation of the provincial governments and the farmers themselves, livestock prices remained steady and the market was able to absorb all livestock offerings throughout the season. The small crop on the prairies, while generally of very high quality, left many farmers short of the necessary working capital for next year's operations. Crop insurance and prairie farm assistance are a welcome help to those farmers who suffered a heavy crop loss. The addition of acreage payments at this time will further assist them and help many who were unable to qualify for the other kinds of assistance.
I listened very carefully the other day to the long speech of the Leader of the Opposition on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sorry that he is not in the chamber at the present time because I thought that as Leader of the Opposition and head of what is supposed to be a national party he would present some of his party's views on agricultural problems. I found it almost beyond belief-

Will the hon. member permit me to point out that the Leader of the Opposition last year expressed his views and those of his party with regard to this $1 an acre assistance. He also outlined our party's views on agricultural policy at the time that the Prime Minister did.

I am glad that he did it last year because if you will permit me to go on with my speech I would point out that he apparently considered that last year the government had done everything possible for the farmers and therefore it was not necessary for him to mention agriculture at all this year.
He said just the opposite.

As I say, I found it almost beyond belief that he could make this long statement on national affairs without

What did I confirm? I want to make sure of everything that government members say. What did I confirm?
You confirmed that the Liberals have no agricultural policy. I should like to proceed with my speech.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-

In making the acreage payment the government has never regarded it as a handout but as compensation for the low domestic price of wheat to the Canadian consumer. The two-price system has been requested over the years by our farm organizations. The acreage payment has been used as the most equitable manner in which to meet this request. I believe that continuation of this practice by the government will receive the commendation of all fair minded western farmers.

It would not have been necessary, of course, to intervene again but for the frivolous and wholly inaccurate remarks made by the hon. gentlemen who support the minister. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-2, to provide for the establishment of a hospital sweepstakes board.
He said: My purpose in bringing this bill before the house is simply to carry out the wishes of my constituents and those of the vast majority of Canadians by instituting a national hospital sweepstakes.
Of course this is not the first time I have raised this matter in the house. When it came before the house last session a great deal of support was expressed for the bill, and I am not going into all the detail I gave last year. However, I would remind the house that I did refer to the Gallup poll on that occasion, a poll which has become a reliable indicator of public opinion on matters such as this. The last poll they took on this subject indicated that 82 per cent of the people of this country were in favour of a national hospital sweepstake.
There is also evidence of widespread support to be found in various press clippings from newspapers across the country. I do not intend to refer to very many, but this is what some of the headlines say: "Vets Want Legal Lottery", "Ontario Municipalities Want Hospital Sweep", "Ontario Votes for Sweeps". This latter headline was a reference to a vote taken in the Ontario legislature some years ago. Then there is another which says: "Unions Ask for Government Lottery". This referred to a statement by the trade union congress representing some 500,000 people in labour unions across Canada. The statement was made to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which was set up in 1956 to make recommendations on this matter.
Hon. members will recall, too, that I made reference to the fact that sweepstakes were common throughout the world and accepted by people universally. They were not considered by the people generally as gambling in the ordinary sense of the word. We now have various types of gambling in the country some of which, such as betting on horse racing, are legal. In addition, of course, a good many illegal types of gambling go on,

too. One thing is certain: the people have an instinct to make wagers and no one can stop them doing that.
The joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons had before it during its sittings a mounted police commissioner who indicated that the present law was entirely unsatisfactory and could not be enforced, with the result that the law was being brought into disrepute. I recall also referring last session to the evidence of several law enforcement officers in the United States and other countries who had taken the same position indicating that the law could not be supported and that in their opinion some change should be made.
Then, too, it is the essence of a democracy that the wishes of the people should be carried out and I find it difficult to believe that any hon. member of this house could stand up and say that he did not think there was a large body of opinion among the people he represented who were in favour of a hospital sweepstake. This has been reiterated over and over again in the press. One can turn to the newspapers almost any time and read such headlines as: "Fourteen Canadians Draw Tickets in the Irish Sweep". One can read about the number of prizes won and see the actual names of the prize winners in Canada. As I pointed out last session, a large amount of money comes to Canada from this source-over 25 per cent of the total prizes of the last Irish sweepstake. This indicates clearly that we are paying a very large sum of money indeed into the fund, only a small percentage of which comes back. I suggest that this sweepstake is something which is wanted by the people of Canada and it is time that the members of this house accepted their responsibility and carried out the wishes of the people in this respect.
Last year I took the liberty of writing to a number of foreign embassies whose countries conducted national sweepstakes of one sort or another. They were very kind in their replies and sent me the most extensive information. I do not intend to go into detail now with regard to that, because I put it on record in Hansard last year. The details can all be found in Hansard commencing at page 6965. At that time I showed the arguments which had been put forward that hospital sweepstakes were very inefficient and that a large proportion of the money was used up in administrative costs to be completely unfounded on the basis of actual figures which were supplied by the various countries to whose representatives I wrote. They sent me complete details of their schemes and these showed that the administrative costs were very low and were not a serious factor. The money was mainly used
Legislation to Establish Sweepstakes Board for hospital or other charitable purposes or for prizes to the people who bought tickets,
I strongly suggest that whatever action we propose to take or whatever action we fail to take in this house, we shall not stop people from buying sweep tickets. Canadians are now buying Irish sweepstake tickets, tickets in the French national lottery, tickets in the Mexican national lottery and tickets in sweepsakes as far away as New Zealand and Australia. There have been a number of items in the press indicating this to be a fact.
I referred last year to items carried in newspapers in other countries indicating that money from Canada was finding its way abroad. I might mention, again, that a large number of editorials have appeared in newspapers across the country. I have a number of them here but I do not intend to read them because they are far too numerous. However, papers from one end of Canada to another have carried editorials on this subject. Some of them have been strongly in favour of the idea of a national lottery. Others have said they are not too favourably disposed but on the other hand they recognize the desire of the Canadian people to have a national hospital sweepstake and recognize the right of the majority to have its wishes carried out. It was a matter to be considered by this house and carried into effect.
Hon. members will probably recall the attitudes taken by the various provinces on this question. The views of the government of Quebec are well known. They have had them throughout the years, and legislation was passed some years ago to provide for a lottery or sweepstake within that province. The reason I have proposed the type of bill that I have is this: I do not believe that the scheme could work on a provincial basis. The federal government has taken the position on many occasions that payments as between provinces should be equalized as far as possible. It seems to me tremendous problems in law enforcement would be brought about if one or more provinces held their own sweepstakes, because it would be impossible to prevent the sale of tickets in another province. Moreover, the entire balance of payments as between the provinces would be upset. For these reasons I think it best that this should be done on a national basis and that provision should be made in the bill for the profits to be distributed on a per capita basis so that there would be fairness for all throughout Canada. I believe, also, that this would avoid any disagreement between provincial governments because of the upsetting of the balance of payments as between them.
I have no desire to repeat all I said last session, especially as I know there are many

Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of an amendment to the Criminal Code which would permit the establishment of a national lottery to control this outflow of Canadian dollars to the benefit of other countries.
Canadians spend some $90 million each year to buy sweepstake tickets from other countries.
We all remember the referendum held last year by the Montreal La Presse and radio station CKAC about a lottery. In the Montreal area and the province of Quebec, nearly
100,000	people voted for and only 150 against it.
Section 179 of the Criminal Code prohibits lotteries. Does that mean that there are none? Yesterday Canada was the choice land for bingos; today it is a paradise for the organizers of drawings of all sorts. Who does not know a thousand and one ways of evading the law?
Should we draw the conclusion that we should hunt down the organizers of drawings and of all those disguised lotteries?
Why not admit instead that they do meet a need? Boileau, who, in his fashion, was an excellent student of the ways of men, found out long before we did that "since we must go to law, since we must leave this earth, we must have lawyers, we must have doctors".
Quebec is not the only place where Irish sweepstakes and army and navy tickets are sold in the open. Moreover, what Canadian would accept to be judged severely because, at the races, he had dared to bet on such and such a horse?
When brought before the courts, the bingo operators generally ask for a trial by jury. Find me a jury with not a single bingo player.
Canadians spend $225 million dollars per year on gambling, 95 per cent of that amount for bets on horses.
Of the total bets, 70 per cent are made in Ontario, according to a Canadian Bank of Commerce business letter published in 1960.
People will always have a yen for gambling. In my opinion, a lottery would regulate and rectify the present situation and, according to a ruling of the income tax appeal board, winnings from bingo or sweepstakes are not taxed.
It is urgent also that a bill be adopted to allow the Bell Telephone Company of


Canada to withdraw its service from a customer deemed by the attorney general of the province to be using the telephone for illegal gambling purposes.
Mr. Speaker, I want to give some of my colleagues the opportunity to express their opinion on that subject. I fully support the bill under study since I have myself submitted a bill to amend the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-2 is a most interesting bill and contains a basic, major issue of principle. I cannot speak with a knowledge of the thinking of all my colleagues in this corner of the house on this matter of sweepstakes, but I should like to express my own personal opinion.
I am in support of the principle of Bill No. C-2, if only for the reason that we may as well face reality and recognize that it is not possible to legislate the gambling habit out of the human animal. If we cannot legislate it out-and I maintain that we cannot- then surely the sensible thing to do is try to either control or regulate that gambling habit so that it is done in a legal fashion and there is, as far as possible, the guarantee of a decent return for the money gambled. In this way we could see that the money which is expended is put to a proper use in Canada.
If we oppose in principle the matter of a government controlled sweepstake for a humanitarian and beneficial purpose, then we are hypocrites in allowing by law the gambling that goes on at the present time. All across Canada, if you happen to be a member of certain clubs, it is quite legal to play poker or blackjack.
By law every citizen of Canada has the right-and many exercise it-to go to the horse races and gamble millions of dollars annually. In addition, millions of dollars are gambled annually at bingo. Let us not forget that these bingo games, which are strictly games of chance, are held in every province of Canada. They are sponsored by whom? By social clubs, by veterans clubs, by political clubs, by churches. I do not know how much we recognize clubs at which members can play blackjack or poker, but they are all legal; it is all gambling, all games of chance.
I do not know whether it is an inborn, inherent trait of an individual to want to take a chance, but annually we have countless millions of dollars going outside this country, despite all the efforts of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) to stop it, to sweepstakes in Ireland, Australia and other countries. Surely, therefore, we should recognize

Legislation to Establish Sweepstakes Board
all these obvious facts and realities and that we are not going to stop that trait. If people want to buy sweepstake tickets-and they are going to buy them-let them be bought within the law in Canada, under government control, with strict supervision and with a fair share of the money received from the exercise of that gambling spirit going towards a useful humanitarian project within our own country.
I do not think it is the way we should finance hospitals. It is not the way we should finance things which are necessary to Canada. But if it is going to help and we can exercise some control over the gambling instinct and keep the money inside Canada, I think we would be honest not to blind ourselves to what is going on legally in regard to games of chance and say, with regard to sweepstakes, that this cannot be done.
For those reasons, although I know certain people and organizations have objections-because whether they are political clubs, social clubs, veterans clubs or churches, it is permitted in Canada, recognized and sponsored by these people and organizations-let us not be hypocrites in this matter. Let us not deny what we know is a basic human instinct.
We are not going to overthrow this instinct overnight, or for generations, and we must recognize the desire of the majority of people. At least let us give to those who desire it the right to take part in a government-sponsored sweepstake, with the money being held in Canada for the benefit of Canadians and projects in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this subject. It has been referred to as a very popular subject with a great many people in Canada. I think that of all the bills that have come before the house since I have been a member, this is by far the most sound. It seeks to establish a full time board of men who will properly run a sweepstake for the benefit of hospitals in Canada. This sort of thing has been referred to in the past as a type of taxation and some people feel that the poor, or the person who is less able to pay for it, will be taxed the most. This runs against their grain.
As has been pointed out a number of times, most people are already paying in one way or another. They are going out and buying tickets for sweepstakes. Often those sweepstake tickets never get to Ireland. The person from whom they buy the tickets is selling them under cover and sometimes the money is not sent in and the buyer is out of his money. He does not even get the chance, whether it is a fair gamble or not. This type of thing goes on time and again.
If a sweepstake such as this were set up, we in Canada could establish a very workable system. Post offices could sell the tickets without any extra expense. They could be sold almost in the same way that five cent stamps are sold, if a person wishes to buy them. I am not saying they should be priced at five cents, but they could be sold in the post offices and the R.C.M.P. and people behind the project could outlaw all other sweepstakes.
What have we today? We have laws which have not the backing of the people. Quite often when laws are in force and the people are not backing them, those laws turn out to be rather ineffective. This is the case with sweepstakes.
In a small town in my riding a very good friend of mine called me and said, "You know, Jack, it is time we legalized some form of sweepstakes in Canada". I said, "Why?" He said, "Last September I sent $1,200 out of this small town to Ireland". I said, "I did not think it was that much". He said, "Look, there are at least five or seven more fellows in this town of 2,500 selling tickets and I do not know how much money they sent to Ireland". This just gives some idea of the amount of money that is leaving small towns in western Canada to go to Ireland.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) pointed out that 25 per cent of the tickets drawn are held by persons in Canada. I think it is a logical thing to say that we must be sending over to Ireland at least 25 per cent of the money that is taken in. That is an enormous amount of money to be leaving this country. I know it can be said that if we legalize some form of sweepstakes in Canada, money will still be going over to the sweepstakes in Ireland. Perhaps some money might go there. But with the support of the people behind the law with regard to a legalized sweepstake in Canada and with a crackdown by the R.C.M.P. on foreign sweepstakes, I think most of the money would be funnelled into benefits for our own hospital or medical care. Certainly in my own riding people have told me this, "Look, we even sell tickets to the R.C.M.P.; they buy them and put them in their wives' names". I am not saying this in order to discredit our very noble force in Canada. I am pointing this matter out in order to show that most of the people readily accept the sweepstakes idea and take advantage of it in one way or another. Even the person in the lower income bracket goes out and buys a dollar ticket on a car, to play bingo and so on.
With the ever increasing need for money in order to cover the cost of expensive drugs and hospitalization and with chronic illness becoming a big problem in Canada, and with

Legislation to Establish Sweepstakes Board hospitals being set up in a number of small towns to care for some of the elderly people who are chronically ill, we know we shall certainly continue to need large sums of money for hospitalization. While it has been pointed out that this may not be the best method by which to raise that money, nevertheless it is one way in which it could be raised without harming or hindering in any way any large group of people and without curtailing further development of our country as higher taxes on corporations or something like that might mean.
In this House of Commons in recent years few members have spoken against sweepstakes. I certainly think that there is a feeling of general acceptance right across Canada.
I should just like to point out a few of the things that have been brought to my attention over the years with regard to lotteries and gambling. Some time ago a school teacher said to me, "I did not know whether or not we could hold a Christmas raffle in my school so I thought the proper thing to do would be to write to the closest law enforcement body and ask what the situation was". She wrote to them; in fact, she went to see them. She said that the R.C.M.P. officer, I believe it was, said, "Well, you are perfectly able to go ahead and hold your raffle; I know that other schools do it. However, if there is any big trouble caused over it, I will have to step in; but if no trouble is caused, I will not bother with it, and you can probably go ahead". This teacher who wanted to do what was right had to take the risk on her own shoulders, had to break the law in a sense, in order to raise a little bit of money so that she could be Santa Claus under the Christmas tree in that small country school.
I do not think this is the proper approach. I know a raffle had been held in this school for years before this woman became the teacher there. She wished to continue the practice. She did not want to do away with the Christmas concert or anything like that. However, she did not want to be breaking the law at the same time and she went to the trouble of asking the police officer about the matter. He said in effect, "Go ahead; do it at your own risk. If the neighbouring people raise objection or if somebody squawks against it, I shall have to step in, take a look at it and perhaps lay a charge". This is the position in which we are placing good people who want to obey the law. We are placing them in a position in which they have no alternative.
I know of another instance. I may say that I am bringing this matter out in order to point out how people wish to obey the law and to do what is right, but that we as the


law makers in Canada are sometimes placing them in a difficult position. I also know of a group of people who wanted to build a curling rink. Because there had been an on again-off again approach to lotteries in Alberta and because at the same time a group of people were fined for having a lottery to build a curling rink in one town in Alberta, this particular group of people were concerned about the matter. Again they wanted to do what was right and what was within the law.
They wrote to the premier of the province and asked him if they could hold a car raffle in order to build a curling rink in this town. I might add that the curling rink was sadly needed. They wanted to do what was right. In a sense the premier wrote back and said "Legally you cannot do it; but if you do it, very likely nothing will come of it. Very likely you can proceed and you will be all right". This again placed them in the position in which they knew they were breaking the law but that it would probably be all right if they went right ahead and broke it.
When we have in Canada laws for which the people find themselves having no respect and which are broken by them with no trouble arising out of the breaking of them, I say that we should change the laws so that people will have respect for them. In this particular case the community in question did not build a curling rink. However, a community five or six miles up the line a year later went ahead and raffled a car, took a chance of being thrown in jail if anything came of it and they built their curling rink. I may say that curling rink has flourished in that part of the community ever since then.
This is the trouble we have with sweepstakes being readily accepted and the laws not permitting them to be legally operated. Having regard to the experience we have had with sweepstakes, I think that we in Canada should be realistic enough and should have enough knowledge of human nature to go ahead and legalize a sweepstake board, make it the only sweepstake board operating in Canada and make its tickets the only sweepstake tickets allowed to be sold in Canada. If you get the people behind the idea and have it accepted by the general public, they will readily buy tickets for a Canadian sweepstake. They will not likely buy too many foreign sweepstakes tickets if they know they are illegal and that the law is going to be enforced to the hilt with regard to them. We should not have R.C.M.P. officers buying sweepstakes tickets and putting them in their wives' names. Some people think that this is not true and that I am possibly degrading our very able and efficient police force. That is not my intention at all. I am saying this, sir,

to point out the lack of respect that people generally have for the law so far as sweepstakes are concerned.
1 know that two years ago a young fellow in my constituency won $140,000 in the Irish sweepstakes. He had very little when he won the money and he was still looked upon as a respected citizen. Nobody said he was a thief or had broken the law. He was a hero in that particular community. The whole idea of sweepstakes tickets got a shot in the arm there because of his winning. I am proud to say, being a farmer myself, that part of that money was invested in a farm for the young man and I am sure he will make a success of that enterprise. These are the things that we have to consider.
I know that recently in the newspapers at home there has appeared what is called "play at home" bingo. So many numbers are printed each week in the weekly paper. People buy a bingo card for $1 and sit at home and wait eagerly for the weekly paper to come with the numbers for that week. At one time the prize was a thousand dollar bill. I have never had a thousand dollar bill. In the particular town in question the prize was advertised. If you walked by the biggest window of the biggest store in town you could catch a glimpse of the thousand dollar bill in the window on certain days. People buy their cards and play bingo at home in the hope of being the lucky winner. The idea has really gone over. I think the attraction is in the idea of taking a chance by playing bingo and running $1 into $1,000 without even moving off your seat at home but just picking up the weekly paper and filling in the numbers on the bingo card.
A few years ago bingos were looked upon by the province of Alberta with a sceptical eye but today bingo seems to be flourishing again. Alberta seems to blow hot and cold so far as sweepstakes are concerned but people are playing bingo at home. There are now three prizes. The first prize is a thousand dollar bill and the other two prizes are $500 and $200 respectively. This is how widely the idea of bingo and sweepstakes is accepted.
Some time ago in a large city I was asked to speak in a large collegiate or high school. I was going to speak on world affairs in general that night. I happened to walk in the wrong door of the school although I did not realize it at first. There seemed to be quite a crowd gathered there and I thought that surely they had not all come to hear me. Nobody met me at the door and I glanced around and saw that something was being sold and the thought went through my mind that surely they were not charging people to hear me speak because my advice is generally given gratis.
I went up to one of the people at the counter and said, "What is the charge, what goes on?" He said, "It is a bingo. We have a bingo here every week on this day." I was somewhat taken aback so I said to him, "I was to make a speech. Am I in the wrong school or what is the score?" He said, "No, your speech is to be made up on the second floor somewhere and here is a gentleman who will show you where to go." I went up there and made my speech to a crowd of 35 or 40 people, but down below there were 400 or 500 people taking a chance playing bingo. They did so every week for 52 weeks in the year. I do not know for how many years it has been going on. That is how widely accepted the idea is of taking a chance of running a dollar into a five dollar bill or a thousand dollar bill. These people were perhaps concerned about world affairs but not concerned enough to wait until next week to take a chance and come to hear me instead.
This sort of thing flourishes without the provincial governments doing a thing about it because they know that people generally accept the idea of sweepstakes and that it would be practically useless to curtail the practice. I know that the cost of medical care is increasing all the time and at the present time a government inquiry is going on for the purpose of determining how best a medical insurance plan can be worked out for the people of Canada. This also is a popular idea, particularly among persons who are least able to pay for their medical care. Those are the same people who some are trying to protect by keeping sweepstakes illegal. These same people who want hospital and medical care want to gamble. They want to run a dollar into a thousand dollars or a dollar into a five dollar bill. How can we protect them both ways? Certainly we can protect them to a certain extent, as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) said, with regard to how much of their wages they gamble, but even that is a difficult thing to do.
I happen to live next door to a merchant in Ottawa who is in charge of a department in one of the larger department stores. He has told me that once the Connaught race track opens every spring business in the store takes a slight drop.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of this bill. Since I am not a lawyer, I do not pretend, of course, to be very conversant with the law. However, as the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) has just stated, gambling and lotteries are taking place throughout Canada at present whether we like it or not.
I realize that some people like to say that laws are made to be broken; but the fact remains that it is not always pleasant to see that so many offences are committed against laws enacted by the state. There is a basic principle to the effect that within a family, the father and mother must take all the means at their disposal to enforce obedience by their children.
The government is like the father of a family. In my opinion, it is only logical that it should have at its disposal all possible means to ensure the respect of its laws. We all know that gambling and lotteries are taking place in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada. Some lotteries are sponsored by philanthropic organizations, others by sport, recreational or charitable associations. On the other hand, we are aware of the fact that some lotteries benefit only one or two persons. Some lotteries thrive on the public's money and yet the proceeds are intended only for a handful of swindlers.
Mr. Speaker, I quote this sentence from the explanatory notes of the bill:
Accordingly, a board is set up with power to operate sweepstakes on a national scale.
I suggest that the law should be amended in two different ways, the one to broaden its scope, the other to narrow it down.
The scope of the law should be broadened in the sense that honest games and honest lotteries held for charitable or welfare purposes should be permitted. One would then not only be glad to contribute to charity at

home, but, his conscience being clear, he would be happy in the thought that he is abiding by the laws of his country and his province.
On the other hand, the scope of the law should be narrowed down to make it more strict, to have it prohibit severely and thoroughly games and lotteries which are of no benefit to the nation and the people.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that in this way, our people would find deep satisfaction in the knowledge that their government had made it easier for them to respect its laws.

I was speaking of the results obtained in the community chest campaigns across this country this year. The results were disappointing a year ago and I understand they were even more disappointing this year. This is not true of my community, and I am glad to hear it is not true of Ottawa. I believe these community chest campaigns indicate the
Legislation to Establish Sweepstakes Board acceptance by the people of the community of their responsibility under our system. The point I am trying to make is that we all say we like to take a gamble, that the people want to take a gamble, that this money is going out of the country so we should give the people the opportunity to buy the tickets here.
I do not think we can legislate the morals of people, but I do say concern should be expressed somewhere along the line about the apparent growing weakness of our people to contribute legitimately to meet the responsible needs of their communities and their country. If this bill goes through it may be the answer to all the problems of some people, but it may create an awful lot more than they have now. It may leave us holding a bag that we shall have great difficulty filling.
My philosophy is that I would like to see less government and less government spending, regardless of which party forms the government. I would like to see more people stand up and say "we are responsible, we will solve our problems, we will do the job". There is a growing trend today, sponsored by a small group in the far corner of this chamber, a very vociferous group who have a lot of support, though they will not admit it, from another very vociferous group, towards declaiming that governments have an over-all responsibility and that governments can do everything. This trend is weakening our free community. I remember the day when we faced problems involving the lack of food and clothing in small communities in western Canada. Pioneers would come there, raise sod shacks, and the community accepted the responsibility and solved their problems. They did not run to the government and say "Mister, look after me". I regard this tendency as dangerous to our western democracy, and one which could in time make us ripe for communism.
We had an example from the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson). I know he is a gambler-I do not say I am not-and he told us about a man who sold 6,000 books of tickets. I believe that in almost every community in Canada today there are professional sellers of sweepstake tickets. They have a sucker list to whom they can sell any ticket that is printed, but there is no guarantee that the tickets people buy from them are legitimate, or that the buyers have any chance of winning. This is happening all over the country and I would hope if any action is taken by parliament in this connection it would be on such a basis that we would not build up a preferred class of people.

For years I have belonged to community sporting organizations. I think it was the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) who advocated having a national lottery and making everything else illegal. This I would not support. In my community we have one of the top junior A hockey clubs in Canada. In my province we have probably the second best boys' junior hockey league, and we have kept that league alive through community support. In the city of Regina we publish a year book for the benefit of the club, and people I know have subscribed $6,000 a year to the purchases of the club through the year book. This is a substantial acceptance of the responsibility of the community, but we found that in itself it was not enough. Other people in the community, who would have howled to high heaven were the club disbanded and its work among 3,000 boys stopped, gave their assistance when we ran a "young Canadian" night and gave away a car. The tickets for that could be sold any place in the city with ease. This is an area which I believe is deserving of attention where a legitimate purpose can be served.
The prizes which are given away are not huge. The fortunate winners cannot desert their legitimate occupations and start lives of ease, but they are substantial prizes that attract the support of the public and in that way provide much needed money. Organizations such as that, and matters of this kind, should not be overlooked. I do not think anybody misunderstood the reference by the hon. member for Acadia to members of the R.C.M.P. buying sweepstake tickets, but it is
unfortunate that he used that example. They are human like the rest of us. Had he said he was a member of parliament and had a ticket in his pocket for the next sweepstake, it would have been a far better example. I belong to that category and I believe if a poll were taken of the members of the House of Commons it would show almost all of us to be in that category. What is said about the gambling instinct is true, but this is something with which we should not deal without consideration of the over-all picture.

Ottawa, December 23, 1961
The Honourable W. A. C. Bennett, M.L.A., Premier of British Columbia,
Victoria, British Columbia.
My dear Premier:
Before going overseas to the NATO meetings last week, I sent you an interim reply on December 9th to your letter of November 27th concerning the Columbia river treaty. I have now had an opportunity to review the situation.
I would welcome an early resumption of discussions on the financial arrangements, but my colleagues and I feel that it is most important that we should first remove any misunderstanding that may exist about the real purpose of the treaty. In your earlier letter of June 9 you stated that in your view all of Canada's share of the downstream power benefits should be disposed of to the United States. You return to this point in your last letter, and say that it is of paramount importance to you.
This stand is quite contrary to the fundamental purpose of the treaty, which is to secure for the people of British Columbia directly and immediately the cheapest and most abundant electric power available.
I believe it essential to reaffirm the basic position outlined in my letter of May 17 regarding the use which has been clearly envisaged from the beginning on both sides for these power benefits. As you were aware, throughout the negotiation of the treaty, discussions in the Canada-British Columbia policy liaison committee were based on the intention that the bulk of Canada's share of the low cost downstream power benefits would be delivered to Canada for the use and benefit of consumers in British Columbia. The treaty itself accurately reflects this principle. I refer in particular to the following provisions of the treaty:-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
"Article V-Entitlement to downstream power
benefits
(1)	Canada is entitled to one half the downstream power benefits determined under article VII.
(2)	The United States of America shall deliver to Canada at a point on the Canada-United States of America boundary near Oliver, British Columbia, or at such other place as the entities may agree upon, the downstream power benefits to which Canada is entitled, less
(a)	transmission loss,
(b)	the portion of the entitlement disposed of under article VIII (1), and
(c)	the energy component described in article VIII(4)."
"Article VII-Determination of downstream
power benefits
(1)	The downstream power benefits shall be the difference in the hydroelectric power capable of being generated in the United States of America with and without the use of Canadian storage, determined in advance, and is referred to in the treaty as the downstream power benefits.
(2)	For the purpose of determining the downstream power benefits:
(a)	the principles and procedures set out in annex B shall be used and followed;
(b)	the Canadian storage shall be considered as next added to 13,000,000 acre-feet of the usable storage listed in column 4 of the table in annex B;
(c)	the hydroelectric facilities included in the base system shall be considered as being operated to make the most effective use for hydroelectric power generation of the improvement in stream flow resulting from operation of the Canadian storage.
(3)	The downstream power benefits to which Canada is entitled shall be delivered as follows:
(a)	dependable hydroelectric capacity as scheduled by the Canadian entity, and
(b)	average annual usable hydroelectric energy in equal amounts each month, or in accordance with a modification agreed upon under paragraph (4).
(4)	Modification of the obligation in paragraph 3(b) may be agreed upon by the entities."
"Article VIII-Disposal of entitlement to
downstream power benefits
(1) With the authorization of Canada and the United States of America evidenced by exchange of notes, portions of the downstream power benefits to which Canada is entitled may be disposed of within the United
States of America. The respective general conditions and limits within which the entities may arrange initial disposals shall be set out in an exchange of notes to be made as soon as possible after the ratification date.
(2)	The entities may arrange and carry out exchanges of dependable hydroelectric capacity and average annual usable hydroelectric energy to which Canada is entitled for average annual usable hydroelectric energy and dependable hydroelectric capacity respectively.
(3)	Energy to which Canada is entitled may not be used in the United States of America except in accordance with paragraphs (1) and (2)."...
"Article X-East-west stand-by transmission
(1) The United States of America shall provide in accordance with good engineering practice east-west stand-by transmission service adequate to safeguard the transmission from Oliver, British Columbia, to Vancouver, British Columbia, of the downstream power benefits to which Canada is entitled and to improve system stability of the east-west circuits in British Columbia."
These provisions obviously rest on the intention that, in the normal course, our downstream benefits will be physically returned to Canada. I draw your attention to the word "portion" in Article V and the word "portions" in article VIII. At no time prior to the signing of the treaty was it even hinted by you, your ministers, or your officer who was appointed as one of the four negotiators, that your government would demand that Canada's share of downstream benefits be sold in the United States.
The basic purpose of the treaty is to provide large supplies of cheap power and thereby benefit the people of British Columbia and the economy of Canada as a whole through the industrial development and employment which can be expected to result This purpose would be defeated and British Columbia producers put at a competitive disadvantage if the bulk of the low-cost downstream benefit power is committed to the United States for several decades.
The great advantages to Canada of the development and use of the low-cost power of the Columbia are brought out once again in specific terms in a study made of them by the Montreal Engineering Company. I am sending you under separate cover a copy of this report in two volumes, and I am enclosing herewith a departmental memorandum setting forth briefly some of the conclusions reached in this report.
We have accomplished what seemed at many times to be an unattainable objective

when we were able to negotiate for the return to Canada, free, of one half of the downstream benefits. My colleagues and I would hope that you will be able to return to the real purpose of the treaty and agree that the bulk of Canada's downstream benefit power should be brought back for use in British Columbia, with only the temporary surpluses being sold to the United States, as provided in article VIII of the treaty.
I am, as always, ready to meet with you, and invite you to suggest several alternative dates in January for consideration.
Wishing you the compliments of the season, I am,
Yours sincerely,
Donald M. Fleming

November 27th.
The Honourable D. M. Fleming, P.C., Q.C., Minister of Finance,
Confederation Building,
Ottawa 4, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Fleming:
In view of our previous discussions concerning the implementation of the Columbia river treaty, I thought you should be advised, as the year end approaches, of British Columbia's endeavours to see the treaty projects take shape.
First, licensing procedure under the "Water Act" of this province were undertaken by British Columbia power commission commencing the 24th day of June 1961, and hearings were conducted by the water comptroller, Mr. Paget, commencing the 18th day of September and will conclude in all likelihood before the end of this year. The water comptroller's report, we trust, will follow shortly thereafter.
Second, the massive engineering required to give definition to the treaty projects has been under way since November 1960. Three consortiums of engineers have been put to work, each concerned with one of the three treaty projects involving Arrow lake storage, Duncan lake and Mica creek. By the end of this calendar year $4,400,000 will have been expended by British Columbia for these purposes and it is now to be anticipated that definitive engineering will be virtually complete on Duncan lake by early 1962, Arrow lakes by mid-1962 and Mica creek early 1963. Detailed engineering will proceed concurrently with construction when authorized.
The most important question remaining, among a number posed by the treaty, arises under provisions of clause 8 of the treaty and involves the contemplated disposition of Canadian downstream benefit electricity in the United States. I refer especially to this matter among the various factors affecting finance, because you are aware that British Columbia feels that the exchange of notes establishing sale of downstream benefits pursuant to clause 8 is the key to Canadian financial wellbeing. Canada's position is, of course, in effect to be assumed and discharged by British Columbia. Therefore this matter is of paramount importance to us in arranging finance.
My purpose in writing is to suggest that time and events are becoming appropriate for our respective financial officers to bring themselves up to date on this whole matter. I would appreciate learning from you a date which might be suitable for a further meeting and would be pleased to suggest, if it were convenient to you, that you and your advisers might meet in Victoria, but if this is not possible I shall be glad to meet you in Ottawa. While I am very busy preparing for the opening of our own legislature, and with the preparation of the budget, yet I feel that the treaty should be ratified as soon as possible, and therefore will be pleased to go to Ottawa.
Kindest personal regards,
Yours very truly,
W. A. C. Bennett
Premier
